name: Cariprazine (Vraylar)
summary: Second-generation antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar I disorder (mania and depression), and as an add-on treatment for major depressive disorder. Not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
description: Cariprazine (Vraylar) is an atypical antipsychotic that fine-tunes dopamine and serotonin signaling in the brain. It’s used to treat schizophrenia, manic or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder, bipolar depression, and as an adjunct when antidepressants alone aren’t enough for major depressive disorder. Because it has very long-acting metabolites, it builds up slowly and can keep working for weeks after dose changes or stopping. It is not approved for behavior problems in older adults with dementia-related psychosis due to an increased risk of death in this population.
patient_summary: Vraylar helps with mood swings, severe depression, and symptoms like hearing voices or feeling paranoid. Many people take it for bipolar disorder or schizophrenia, and some use it along with an antidepressant for stubborn depression. It’s taken once a day and builds up gradually in your system, so changes are slow and steady rather than overnight. Common issues are feeling restless, having trouble sitting still, or feeling a bit wired or sleepy. It is not meant for memory problems or behavior changes in dementia.

primary_indications: Bipolar I Disorder – acute mania and mixed episodes

linked_conditions.context: Approved for schizophrenia to help with hallucinations, disorganized thinking, and lack of motivation.
Used for acute manic or mixed episodes and bipolar depression in bipolar I disorder.
Added to antidepressants in adults when response to antidepressant alone is incomplete.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity (rash, hives, angioedema) to cariprazine or formulation components
Use with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers in some regions (eg, Canadian labeling)

efficacy_response.patient_text: In clinical trials, more people taking Vraylar had meaningful improvements in mood and psychotic symptoms compared to placebo, particularly for bipolar mania, bipolar depression, and schizophrenia.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed by mouth with peak levels in about 3–6 hours
pharmacokinetics.onset: Initial benefit often within 1–2 weeks depending on condition
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP3A4 and, to a lesser extent, CYP2D6 to active metabolites (DCAR and DDCAR)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (about 21% of dose, ~1% as unchanged drug)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken with or without food

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Cariprazine is used for serious mood and thought disorders where dopamine and serotonin signaling are out of balance.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Hallucinations, paranoia, disorganized thinking, emotional flatness.
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar I Disorder – Mania or Mixed Episodes}: High energy, little sleep, racing thoughts, irritability, risky behavior.
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar I Depression}: Very low mood, slowed thinking, low energy, guilt, or hopelessness.
{link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder}: Used as an add-on when antidepressants alone are not enough.

sections.heading: What People Commonly Notice
sections.intro: People’s experiences vary, but these are common patterns reported in real-world use:

quotes: My thoughts slowed down enough that I could follow a conversation again.
The highs weren’t as out of control and the lows weren’t as bottomless.
I felt more like myself instead of being run by my symptoms.
At first I felt like I had to move constantly, like my body couldn’t sit still.
The inner restlessness was annoying, but it eased after a few weeks.
We had to tweak the dose when the pacing got too uncomfortable.
items.note: This feeling of needing to move (akathisia) often appears in the first weeks and may improve with time or dose adjustments.

quotes: Some days I felt a little drowsy; other days I felt wired.
Once the dose settled, my sleep got more predictable.
I had to learn what time of day worked best for taking it.
My appetite changed a bit, but not as dramatically as with some other meds.
I did gain a little weight, so we’re watching my diet and labs.
items.note: Cariprazine has a lower metabolic risk than some antipsychotics, but weight and labs still need monitoring.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Because cariprazine and its active metabolites stay in the body for a long time, changes are gradual—both when starting and when stopping.
key_points: Bipolar mania or mixed episodes: Some improvement often noticed within days, with more clear benefit over 1–2 weeks.
Bipolar depression: Early benefit may appear within about 1 week, with continued improvement over 6 weeks.
Adjunctive treatment in major depression: Initial change within 1–2 weeks, more robust results over 6–12 weeks.
Schizophrenia: Early response is often seen in 1–2 weeks, with continued improvement over 4–6 weeks.
Because of long-acting metabolites, steady state and full effect may take several weeks, and side effects can also emerge late.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Across trials in schizophrenia, bipolar I mania/mixed states, bipolar depression, and major depressive disorder, cariprazine consistently outperformed placebo for reducing core symptoms such as hallucinations, disorganized thinking, elevated mood, irritability, and depressive symptoms. Benefits are most apparent when it is titrated carefully and continued long enough to reach steady state.
sections.clinical_details: Cariprazine has been studied as monotherapy for schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder (mania and mixed features), and as adjunctive therapy to antidepressants in major depressive disorder. Doses above labeled maximums (eg, 12 mg/day) have not shown greater benefit but may increase adverse effects such as akathisia and extrapyramidal symptoms. Because of very long-acting metabolites, both efficacy and side effects can lag behind dose changes by several weeks.

citation.title: Clinical trials of cariprazine in schizophrenia, bipolar I disorder, and major depressive disorder

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Not approved for behavior problems in older adults with dementia. In this group, antipsychotics increase the risk of death.
sections.black_box: Elderly people with dementia-related psychosis who are treated with antipsychotic drugs have a higher risk of death, mostly from heart problems or infections. Cariprazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Antidepressants can raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults; cariprazine is sometimes used with antidepressants, so careful monitoring is essential. Vraylar is not approved for use in children.
other: May cause sudden or delayed suicidal thoughts or behavior changes, especially when used with antidepressants and early in treatment or after dose changes.
Can cause movement disorders (stiffness, tremor, restlessness, tardive dyskinesia). Some movement problems can become long-lasting.
May worsen or trigger neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but life-threatening reaction with fever, rigidity, and confusion.
May contribute to weight gain, elevated blood sugar, and cholesterol changes over time.
Can cause dizziness or drops in blood pressure, especially when first starting or increasing the dose, increasing the risk of falls.
Can lower seizure threshold in people with seizure risk.
Plasma levels build up slowly; adverse effects may appear weeks after starting or changing dose.
patient_counseling: This medicine is not for memory problems or behavior changes in dementia. It can be dangerous in that setting.
Tell your prescriber right away if you or a loved one notice new or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, severe agitation, or sudden behavior changes.
Report any severe restlessness (feeling like you can’t sit still), muscle stiffness, unusual movements, or shaking.
Seek emergency help for high fever, heavy sweating, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, or dark urine—these can be signs of a rare reaction called neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Keep all lab and follow-up appointments to monitor weight, blood sugar, cholesterol, and movement side effects.
Do not stop abruptly unless you are told to do so for safety reasons. Most of the time, doses should be reduced slowly.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most people tolerate cariprazine fairly well, but restlessness, movement changes, and stomach upset are common. Serious reactions are rare but can be life-threatening.
plain_language_list: Feeling restless or like you have to keep moving (akathisia).
Stiffness, shaking, or other movement changes (extrapyramidal symptoms).

common.patient_note: Often appears in first 2–6 weeks or after dose increases; can feel like you ‘can’t sit still’. Dose changes or add-on treatments sometimes help.
Range from mild stiffness or shakiness to more disabling movement changes; usually improve with dose adjustments or medications, but can occasionally persist.
Often improves with time; hydration, sleep, and dose timing may help.
May feel wired at night or sleepy in the day until your body adjusts.
Taking with food and slow dose increases may help; let your prescriber know if persistent.
Usually mild compared with some other antipsychotics but still important to monitor with weight, labs, and lifestyle.
May be worse at higher doses; timing the dose or adjusting the dose can sometimes help.

serious: Tardive dyskinesia: Involuntary movements of face, tongue, or body that may become permanent.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: High fever, rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure and heart rate; medical emergency.
Severe extrapyramidal symptoms: Very stiff muscles, difficulty moving, problems swallowing or speaking.
Falls and injuries due to dizziness, sedation, or low blood pressure when standing.
Severe changes in blood sugar or lipids, new or worsening diabetes (rare but possible).
Low white blood cell counts (leukopenia, neutropenia), which can increase infection risk.
Seizures in people with lowered seizure threshold.
Severe rash or skin reaction (very rare).
Sudden worsening of mood, new suicidal thoughts, or dangerous impulsive behavior.

sections.heading: Important Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Cariprazine is processed mainly by the liver enzyme CYP3A4. Drugs that strongly affect this pathway can dramatically change its levels.

items.with: Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (eg, certain antifungals, some macrolide antibiotics, some HIV medications)
items.risk: Can raise cariprazine levels and increase side effects (especially restlessness, movement problems, and sedation).
items.action: In some regions (eg, Canada) combination is not recommended. In general, prescribers may avoid combination or adjust doses very cautiously.

items.with: Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inducers (eg, some seizure medicines, rifampin, St. John’s wort)
items.risk: Can lower cariprazine levels and reduce effectiveness.
items.action: Avoid if possible; prescribers may choose a different antipsychotic if a strong inducer is needed.

items.with: Other medications that cause drowsiness or lower blood pressure
items.risk: Increased risk of sedation, dizziness, falls, and blood pressure drops on standing.
items.action: Use caution, rise slowly from sitting or lying positions, and report frequent lightheadedness or falls.

items.risk: Higher risk of movement disorders, NMS, and metabolic side effects.
items.action: Usually avoided unless carefully planned cross-tapering is being done by a psychiatry specialist.

sections.heading: Stopping or Switching Safely
sections.text: Because cariprazine and its active metabolites hang around in the body for a long time, both stopping and switching need planning.
key_points: In long-term treatment, switching to another antipsychotic is usually safer than suddenly stopping all antipsychotics.
If you need to stop Vraylar, prescribers typically lower the dose gradually over weeks to months when possible.

Stopping suddenly can lead to rebound symptoms (return of psychosis or mood episodes) and withdrawal-like symptoms such as agitation, anxiety, insomnia, flu-like feelings, or temporary movement problems.
When switching from another antipsychotic, strategies include cross-taper (slowly lowering the old drug while raising Vraylar) or, less commonly, abrupt switch depending on clinical situation.
Because of its slow clearance, symptoms and side effects from Vraylar may continue to change for weeks after dose changes or discontinuation.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Adults)
sections.text: Cariprazine is usually taken once daily, with or without food. Doses are increased slowly to balance benefit and side effects.

adult.elderly: Avoid for dementia-related behavior. For older adults with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or major depression, start at the low end of the range, increase slowly, and monitor closely for side effects, falls, and cognitive changes.
adult.hepatic: Mild to moderate liver impairment (Child-Pugh A or B): no routine starting dose adjustment, but titrate slowly and monitor closely. Use is not recommended in severe liver impairment (Child-Pugh C).
adult.renal: No dose adjustment is needed for CrCl ≥30 mL/minute. Use is not recommended for severe kidney impairment (CrCl <30 mL/minute) because it has not been studied.

sections.simple_explanation: Your prescriber will usually start low and move up in small steps every few days to weeks, depending on how you feel and what you can tolerate. Because the medication stays in your system a long time, dose changes take time to show up.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Cariprazine has limited data in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Decisions should be individualized with a specialist.
sections.pregnancy: Overall, second-generation antipsychotics do not appear to dramatically increase the risk of major birth defects, but data for cariprazine itself are limited. Using any antipsychotic in the third trimester can cause temporary withdrawal or movement symptoms in newborns (such as agitation, abnormal tone, feeding problems, or breathing issues). Untreated psychosis, depression, or bipolar disorder also carries serious risks for parent and baby. Treatment choices should be made through shared decision-making with psychiatry and obstetrics, using the lowest effective dose and avoiding unnecessary polypharmacy.
sections.lactation: It is not known if cariprazine passes into human breast milk. Other antipsychotics can appear in breast milk and may cause sleepiness, feeding difficulties, or slowed development in infants. Decisions about breastfeeding while on Vraylar should weigh the benefits of breastfeeding, the importance of treatment for the parent, and the potential risks for the infant. If breastfeeding continues, monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, poor weight gain, or unusual movements.
sections.pediatrics: Safety and effectiveness have not been established in people under 18 years old. Second-generation antipsychotics can increase risks of weight gain, diabetes, abnormal lipids, and hyperprolactinemia in children and teens. Use is generally avoided outside of research or specialist-directed care.
sections.geriatrics: In adults ≥65 years, especially those with dementia, antipsychotics increase the risk of stroke, cognitive decline, and death. Vraylar is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. In older adults with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or depression, start with very low doses, titrate slowly, and monitor closely for EPS, falls, hyponatremia/SIADH, and metabolic changes.
sections.hepatic: Use with caution in mild to moderate liver impairment and avoid in severe impairment. Monitor liver function tests periodically.
sections.renal: Use with caution in reduced kidney function; avoid when CrCl <30 mL/minute due to lack of data.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Symptom control and adherence at every visit.
Blood pressure, pulse, temperature, and signs of infection at each visit early in treatment and after dose changes.
Weight, height, and BMI at baseline; again at 8 and 12 weeks; then at least every 3–6 months. Consider waist circumference yearly in those at metabolic risk.
Fasting blood glucose or HbA1c and lipid panel about 4 months after starting and at least annually (or more often if abnormal).
Ask about symptoms of high prolactin (changes in periods, libido, breast changes, sexual dysfunction); check levels if symptomatic.
Watch for extrapyramidal symptoms and akathisia at every visit; use a formal movement rating scale at least annually, or every 6 months if high risk.
Screen for tardive dyskinesia at every visit; use a formal scale (eg, AIMS) at least yearly or more often if risk factors present.
Review fall risk, especially in older adults, at each visit.
CBC as clinically indicated, particularly if there is a history of low white blood cell counts or drug-induced neutropenia.
Metabolic syndrome history and cardiovascular risk factors annually.

Consider therapeutic drug monitoring in special situations to assess adherence or unexplained side effects; a reference trough range of about 10–20 ng/mL has been proposed, with alert levels above ~40 ng/mL.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Cariprazine comes as oral capsules in several strengths.
items: US: Capsules 1.5 mg, 3 mg, 4.5 mg, 6 mg; therapy packs may include 1.5 mg and 3 mg capsules for titration.
Canada: Capsules 1.5 mg, 3 mg, 4.5 mg, 6 mg; dye content varies slightly by strength and country.
No generic equivalent is currently available in the US.

sections.heading: How It Works in the Brain
sections.text: Cariprazine is a second-generation antipsychotic that partially stimulates some dopamine and serotonin receptors while blocking others. It acts as a partial agonist at dopamine D2 and D3 receptors and serotonin 5-HT1A receptors, and as an antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2A and 5-HT2B receptors. It also binds to histamine H1 receptors and has low activity at certain adrenergic receptors, with essentially no activity at muscarinic (cholinergic) receptors. By fine-tuning dopamine and serotonin signaling, it helps stabilize mood, reduce psychosis, and improve thinking without fully shutting down dopamine transmission.

sections.heading: Where It Fits in Treatment
sections.text: Cariprazine is often chosen when a partial dopamine agonist is desired for schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder, or when depression has not responded adequately to antidepressants alone. Compared to some older antipsychotics, it tends to cause less sedation and fewer metabolic problems, but restlessness and movement-related side effects are more prominent and require careful monitoring. Because of its long half-life and delayed steady state, prescribers usually avoid frequent dose changes and instead give each adjustment time to take full effect.

seo.title: Cariprazine (Vraylar): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Warnings
seo.description: Learn how Vraylar (cariprazine) is used for schizophrenia, bipolar I disorder, and treatment-resistant depression—plus common side effects, black box warnings, dosing, and monitoring.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content rewritten for the general public from specialist sources, while preserving key safety information and psychiatric clinical context.

faqs.a: Cariprazine (Vraylar) is used to treat schizophrenia, manic or mixed episodes in bipolar I disorder, bipolar depression, and as an add-on medicine for major depressive disorder in adults whose symptoms are not fully controlled by antidepressants alone.

faqs.q: How long does Vraylar take to start working?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes within 1 to 2 weeks, especially with mania. For bipolar depression, major depression, and schizophrenia, it often takes several weeks to see full benefit. Because the drug and its metabolites last a long time in the body, improvements and side effects can both be delayed.

faqs.q: Why do I feel like I can’t sit still after starting Vraylar?
faqs.a: A common side effect called akathisia can cause inner restlessness and an urge to move. It often shows up in the first few weeks or after dose increases. Tell your prescriber if this happens—dose adjustments or add-on treatments may help.

faqs.q: Is Vraylar safe for older adults with dementia?
faqs.a: No. Like other antipsychotics, Vraylar can increase the risk of death and stroke in older adults with dementia-related psychosis and is not approved for this use. For older adults with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or depression, it may be used carefully at low doses with close monitoring.

You should not stop Vraylar on your own unless there is an emergency side effect. Stopping suddenly can lead to return of symptoms (such as hallucinations or mood swings) and withdrawal-like effects (such as agitation, insomnia, or movement changes). Work with your prescriber on a slow taper or a planned switch to another medication.

faqs.q: Will Vraylar make me gain weight?
faqs.a: Cariprazine has a lower risk of weight gain and metabolic problems than some other antipsychotics, but some people do gain weight or develop changes in blood sugar or cholesterol. Your weight and labs should be checked regularly, especially in the first few months.

faqs.q: Is Vraylar safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Data specific to Vraylar are limited. Antipsychotics as a group do not appear to dramatically increase birth defect risk, but they can cause temporary withdrawal or movement symptoms in newborns if used late in pregnancy. It isn’t known if Vraylar passes into breast milk. Decisions about pregnancy and breastfeeding on Vraylar should be made with your psychiatrist and obstetric provider, weighing the risks of untreated illness against medication risks.
